paper_title: Loopback Transformer: Towards a Unified View of Residual Looped Transformers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks, but parameter sharing alone does not determine how the results of repeated computation are reused. We take the depth-memory view of residual connections and analyze which representation is stored after each block application and how later reads weight it. A full block output contains both its input and its new update, so weighting that output also reweights the history already carried by the input. Reading individual updates instead, with the shared stack's input kept on a separate path, gives separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer implements these controls: geometric decay sets the total update weight and supplies a recency prior, and attention learns how to allocate that weight. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss than standard Transformer baselines with 40-75% of their Transformer parameters (excluding token embeddings and the output head) at reference scales from 191M to 3B, with training tokens and executed depth matched. It also has higher mean accuracy over thirteen downstream tasks at 1.4B and 3B. At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean among the standard Transformer and seven looped residual designs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Looped Transformers reduce parameter count by repeatedly applying shared blocks to an evolving hidden representation (Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019). Sharing separates computational depth from the number of distinct blocks and supports latent reasoning and inference-time scaling (Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2026). Each visit applies the same transformation to different hidden state and so produces different update. Parameter sharing fixes which transformation is reused; it leaves open how the updates from successive visits are stored, carried forward, and used. Residual connections turn depth into form of memory: each layer writes new computation into residual stream carried forward to later layers. Standard residual addition accumulates block updates with fixed unit coefficients (He et al., 2016), whereas Attention Residuals (AttnRes) learns how to weight these updates and the input (Team et al., 2026). Hyper-Connections (HC) and Hyperloop introduce learned pathways across residual streams or loop visits (Zhu et al., 2025a; Zeitoun et al., 2026). This depth-memory view (Team et al., 2026) connects residual design to linear attention and related recurrent models. Linear attention expresses attention over token history as writes to and reads from recurrent memory (Katharopoulos et al., 2020); RetNet and Mamba-2 additionally control how that memory is retained across steps (Sun et al., 2023; Dao & Gu, 2024). We use this writetransportread perspective to analyze repeated computation along depth. Here, each block produces new write from representation assembled from earlier writes, so the memory rule also influences subsequent computation. We therefore examine what is stored and how memory transitions and readout determine each updates contribution. Seen this way, common residual designs tie together quantities that could be controlled separately. First, full block output contains both its input and its new update. Weighting that output therefore also weights the history carried by the input. Storing updates separately lets the reader assign coefficient directly to each update. Second, joint softmax over the original input and stored updates makes them compete for fixed total weight. Ordinary addition instead fixes the input coefficient but assigns every update weight one, so total update weight grows with the number of block applications. We therefore want separate controls over input strength, total update weight, and allocation across updates. The Loopback Transformer is built around these three controls. It stores individual block updates rather than full block outputs and keeps the shared stacks input on separate path with coefficient one. Geometric decay assigns baseline weight to each update. softmax reader redistributes their total weight according to update content, using the decay weights as recency prior. This separates total update weight from allocation without changing the shared blocks or their token-axis attention. We compare against the standard Transformer, which uses distinct parameters at every layer (labeled Standard in tables and figures), and against seven looped residual designs, always at the same budget of training tokens and the same executed depth. On ClimbMix (Diao et al., 2026), Loopback reaches lower validation loss and higher thirteen-task mean than Standard at 191M, 374M, 778M, 1.4B, and 3B while storing 4075% of its Transformer parameters (Tables 2, 4 and 9 and Fig. 1). At 191M, 374M, and 778M, it also has the lowest validation loss and the highest thirteen-task mean of all nine designs  (Table 2)  . We make three contributions: We connect residual designs with linear attention and related recurrent models by adapting their memory-update rules from token sequences to network depth. The resulting framework describes what each block writes and how its contribution is transported and read. Within this framework, we design the Loopback Transformer, which adds weighted sum of block updates to the original loop input. Geometric decay keeps the total update weight bounded as visits increase at fixed stack size. Attention adjusts each updates weight according to its content while preserving the total. On ClimbMix, Loopback reaches lower validation loss and higher zero-shot task means than matched-depth standard Transformers at five scales from 191M to 3B, with 4075% of their Transformer parameters.

sections.title: 3 RESIDUAL CONNECTIONS AS DEPTH MEMORY
sections.content: Following the depth-memory view (Team et al., 2026), we describe residual connections and recurrent memory by the same write, transport, and read operations. We first compare full block outputs with individual block updates as the stored value, then expand the recurrence to see how the original input and earlier block updates enter later hidden states. The expansion is what we use to compare how existing residual designs reuse earlier computation, and it leads to the design of Loopback.

sections.title: 4 LOOPBACK TRANSFORMER
sections.content: Storing block updates separately allows each read weight to act directly on one update. Loopback uses this representation to form each new hidden state from the original loop input h0 and weighted sum of past block updates  (Fig. 3)  . Geometric decay bounds their total weight as loop iterations increase, while attention adjusts their relative weights using update content. The input stays outside this allocation with coefficient one, preserving the usual residual identity path: if all updates vanish, the shared stack returns h0. Only the residual aggregation changes; the shared blocks are unchanged.

sections.title: 4.1 GEOMETRIC DECAY SETS THE PRIOR AND TOTAL WEIGHT
sections.content: High representation similarity has been observed across depth in Pre-Norm Transformers and across iterations in looped Transformers (Zhu et al., 2025a; Zeitoun et al., 2026). If successive block updates share common component, ordinary residual addition reinforces that component at every iteration. Decay limits this accumulation by shrinking the weights of earlier updates. The decay-only reference accumulates updates within each loop iteration and applies fixed retention 0 < λ 1 at its end.

sections.title: 5 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate parameter efficiency, residual designs, and readers on ClimbMix (Diao et al., 2026). Main comparisons match training tokens and executed depth within each scale. Scale names and the 20-tokens-per-parameter (TPP) budget use Standards total parameters; Transformer counts exclude embeddings and the vocabulary head. Training and evaluation details are in Section D. Baselines. The standard Transformer uses independent blocks; Plain Loop repeats shared blocks with ordinary addition. HC learns full stream mixing, mHC uses Sinkhorn-normalized transport, Hyperloop uses diagonal transport, and iHC uses identity transport with learned read and write gates  (Table 1)  . AttnRes and MHAR are our loop-level adaptations of Attention Residuals and multi-head attention residuals (Team et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026b). Adapters act only inside the loop. Looped arms share the topology and learning rate within each setting; adapter placement and memory sources differ.

sections.title: 5.1 PARAMETER-EFFICIENT LANGUAGE MODELING
sections.content: We first test whether Loopback can achieve lower validation loss than depth-matched standard Transformers with fewer Transformer parameters. Table 2 compares all nine rules at 191M with 20 layers, 374M with 32 layers, and 778M with 48 layers. Loopback stores 40.0%, 56.3%, and 56.3% of the standard baselines Transformer parameters, respectively, and attains the lowest validation loss at all three. Its losses are 0.005, 0.039, and 0.024 nats lower than those of the standard Transformer, respectively. mHC is the closest looped baseline at all three, trailing Loopback by 0.006, 0.011, and 0.005 nats. At 374M with 24 layers, Loopback stores 58.3% of the standard baselines Transformer parameters and again has the lowest loss among the nine rules  (Table 12)  . AttnRes trails Loopback by 0.022 nats at 191M and 0.009 nats at 374M with 24 layers. Figure 4 shows the training-loss curves of Loopback and the standard Transformer across all five model scales.

We evaluate these 20-TPP checkpoints on general benchmarks and mathematical and code tasks. Tests of additional loop iterations also include 191M and 374M models for comparison with Plain Loop.

sections.title: 5.2.1 GENERAL BENCHMARKS
sections.content: Figure 5 summarizes Transformer parameter counts, validation loss, and the thirteen-task zero-shot mean. sections.title: 5.2.2 CODE AND MATHEMATICAL EVALUATION
sections.content: We test whether shared computation improves the modeling of mathematical and code solutions with fewer Transformer parameters. At matched training tokens and executed depth, reference-solution loss on GSM8K, MATH-500, HumanEval, and MBPP measures how well the model predicts worked solution given the problem. Five-shot numeric-answer accuracy on six word-problem sets separately tests final-answer correctness. Loopback has lower solution loss on all four datasets at both large scales  (Table 3)  . At 3B, word-problem accuracy rises from 2.6% to 6.4%. The nine-design comparisons at 191M and 374M also give Loopback the lowest four-set mean  (Table 13)  . Evaluation protocols are in Section G.

sections.title: 5.4 DEPTH AT FIXED PARAMETERS
sections.content: We ask whether Loopbacks validation-loss advantage persists when fixed parameter budget is allocated to different widths and depths, instead of depending on one chosen topology. At 374M and 778M, we train every configuration from scratch, holding training tokens fixed and total parameters approximately fixed while trading width for depth from 16 to 64 layers. Our loop visits stay fixed at two. We compare the standard Transformer and the eight looped rules at every depth (Fig. 7, Table 12, Section F). The effect of added depth differs across residual rules. The standard Transformer loses ground as it gets deeper and narrower: it is best at 24 layers and, at 64, is 0.076 worse at 374M and 0.035 worse at 778M. Among the looped rules, Loopback is lowest at nine of the ten points, and its best tested depth moves from 24 layers at 374M to 48 at 778M. At the sweep endpoints, its margin over the standard Transformer increases from 0.003 at 16 layers to 0.073 at 64 layers at 374M, and from 0.002 to 0.028 at 778M. Figure 7: Depth at fixed parameters. sections.title: 5.5 LINEAR ATTENTION AND RECURRENT MEMORY IN LOOPED TRANSFORMERS
sections.content: We adapt the nine recurrent cores, Mesa, and LaCT-inspired reader in Table 1 to visit boundaries at 191M and 374M, leaving token attention unchanged. Each reader uses either cumulative visit states or whole-visit updates; both interfaces initialize to Plain Loop (Section B.4). The update interface gives lower validation loss in all 22 familyscale comparisons (Fig. 8 and Table 11). Every update-based reader improves on Plain Loop, but the best readers still trail Loopback by 0.0302 nats at 191M and 0.0285 at 374M. These results favor updates over states as the memory value. Fixed-state recurrent cores keep one practical advantage for long loops: each new write is absorbed without rereading the history, and the state does not grow with the visit count. We have not tested whether optimized recurrent kernels turn this into lower memory traffic or higher throughput in deeply looped models.

sections.title: 5.6 EFFICIENCY: COMPUTE, THROUGHPUT, AND MEMORY
sections.content: Loopbacks residual aggregation adds only 0.040.08% forward FLOPs over Standard at matched executed depth in the three measured configurations (Fig. 9 and Table 15). These extra operations normalize and score stored updates, form their weighted sum, and apply decay and mixture replacement; they introduce no Q/K/V projections or extra block evaluations. With our fused implementation, 3B training throughput is 6% below Standards on the same eight H100 GPUs with the same batch layout. Detailed runtime and memory measurements are reported in Section I.

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Parameter sharing and residual reuse. Models with shared depth use weight tying (Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019), relaxed tying with low-rank adaptations (Bae et al., 2025), latent reasoning (Saunshi et al., 2025; Geiping et al., 2026), and adaptive recursion (Bae et al., 2026). Hyperloop learns connections between loop visits (Zeitoun et al., 2026). Residual pathways use gating, addition, and concatenation (Srivastava et al., 2015; He et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2018), scaling (Bachlechner et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024), depth mixtures (Bapna et al., 2018), multi-stream mixing (Zhu et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025), and attention-based aggregation (Team et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026a;b). Storing updates is not new; what we add is the split of update coefficients into input strength, total weight, and allocation, and an account of how each design constrains them. Attention and recurrent memory. Sequence memory includes attention and additive fast weights (Vaswani et al., 2017; Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Schlag et al., 2021), retention and gating (Sun et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Qin et al., 2024), structured state-space dynamics (Gu et al., 2021; Gu & Dao, 2023; Dao & Gu, 2024), delta-rule corrections (Yang et al., 2024; 2025; Team et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025), and optimization-based memory (Von Oswald et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026). We adapt these operations along depth, retaining each blocks token attention; results concern residual interfaces, not the original architectures efficiency.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present Loopback, residual design for parameter-efficient looped Transformers. We connect residual computation with linear attention and recurrent memory by treating successive block applications as memory steps along depth: each application writes new computation, which later blocks access through the residual connection. Loopback stores each blocks update separately and reads this history with attention. The read starts from geometrically decayed weights and redistributes them according to content without changing their sum; the weighted updates are then added to the original loop input. Across the 191M, 374M, 778M, 1.4B, and 3B scales, Loopback improves aggregate quality over matched-depth standard Transformer baselines while using 4075% of their Transformer parameters, excluding token embeddings and the output head. In looped models, how the results of shared computation are retained and reused matters as much as which blocks are shared.

sections.title: 8 LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Our evidence is limited to ClimbMix pretraining at the tested scales and budgets, with single-run large-scale comparisons. The input coefficient is fixed at one; we have not tried learned or layerspecific input injection. Explicit history adds memory traffic and activations, so parameter savings need not reduce latency or peak memory. Extra visits have not improved validation loss. Next steps are other pretraining corpora, controlled comparisons of the reader interfaces, compact memories, and training with variable visit count.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work studies the architecture of language models. All models have at most 3B parameters and are trained on ClimbMix, public pretraining corpus, with evaluation on public benchmarks; no new data were collected and no human subjects were involved. The models are research artifacts that inherit the biases of their training corpus and are not intended for deployment. The method reduces stored parameters at matched executed depth and does not alter the risks associated with language models in general.

sections.content: Inference measurements. One H100 runs each model eagerly with bf16 weights and no gradients; Loopback uses fused reads. Prefill is one forward pass over batch of eight 4,096-token sequences that keeps only the last positions logits and materializes no KV cache, so its measured peak covers weights and transient activations. For Loopback these include the depth history, which exists only within forward pass and is never cached across decoding steps. Loopbacks prefill throughput relative to the standard Transformer is 0.68, 0.72, and 0.81 at 191M, 374M, and 778M.
